```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE,warning=FALSE,message=FALSE)
root <- if (dir.exists('results/summary')) 'results/summary' else '.'
s <- readRDS(file.path(root,'summary.rds'))
p <- s$performance
tab <- function(x,digits=3) knitr::kable(x,digits=digits,row.names=FALSE)
primary <- c('Conditional M-MOM Wald','Stage2 influence Wald','Full influence Wald',
             'Full person percentile','Legacy OLS stacked HC0 (t)','Legacy OLS stacked HC3 (t)')
compact <- function(arm,effect) {
 x <- p[p$arm==arm & p$gamma==effect & p$method%in%primary,]
 x <- x[order(match(x$profile,s$profiles$profile),match(x$method,primary)),]
 x <- x[,c('profile','method','available','coverage','rejection','median_width')]
 names(x) <- c('Profile','Method','Intervals / 100','Coverage','Zero exclusion','Median width')
 x
}
```

## Findings and practical implications

The full influence calculation now follows the actual REPAIR M-MOM estimator,
including estimated measurement parameters, structural weights, corrections and
the signed cross-stage covariance. Its implementation passes independent
likelihood, frequency-perturbation, reoptimization and OLS special-case checks.
**Correct variance propagation alone does not fix the difficult finite-sample
inference in this screen.** Keep the method experimental; the results support
retaining person-level bootstrap inference as the practical alternative in these
settings, while reporting its remaining failures and bias limitations.

- Full influence inference returned **1,351 / 2,400** structural analyses.
  There were 1,048 refusals at singular measurement covariances and one unstable
  parameter derivative. Stage2 influence inference returned all 2,400.
- For the nonzero noisy-predictor effect, low-information full-influence coverage
  ranged from **73.2% to 83.3%** among 37–66 available intervals per profile.
  Bootstrap coverage ranged from **79.4% to 95.8%** among 95–98 intervals.
  Availability differs, so the report also supplies matched-eligible contrasts.
  In three profiles these favor bootstrap coverage by about 11–17 percentage
  points, with paired Monte Carlo intervals excluding zero; this exploratory
  screen is not an adjusted multiple-comparison or confirmatory study.
- In the high-reliability noisy-predictor control all methods returned 100
  intervals; full influence coverage was 92%, bootstrap 91%, conditional 94%.
  A coverage near 95% has Monte Carlo SE about 2.2 percentage points at Nsim=100.
  These differences do not establish superiority.
- In balanced random-slope-outcome analyses, the focal full and stage2 variance
  reduce to OLS HC0. Across 1,000 balanced legacy comparisons, point estimates
  agreed within 5.6e-16 and stage2/legacy HC0 variances within 6.1e-8. The old
  helper's HC corrections and t reference are distinct finite-sample choices;
  their performance must not be attributed to cross-stage propagation.
- The small/short noisy-predictor profile still had point bias about −.207 at
  truth .40, and bootstrap coverage only 79.4%. None of these SE methods removes
  that bias. Bootstrap availability or smaller analytic SEs do not establish
  calibrated inference.

## Design, estimands, and comparability

This is a **paired exploratory extension of the existing robust-refit screen**,
reusing 600 measurement datasets: six profiles × 100 outer replications. Each
dataset supplies two structural designs (arms A/B), each with truths 0 and .40.
These are 2,400 structural analyses, not 2,400 independent measurement datasets.
Streams and native fitting decisions are shared across the comparisons. Main
bootstrap B=499; the fixed first three datasets/profile extend to B=1,999.
Excluded development/timing data use replication 801. The protocol in design.md
was frozen before inspecting full-grid influence performance.

```{r profiles}
tab(s$profiles)
```

The Gaussian measurement model is
Y=.5*time+b0+b1*time+eps. Within-person time is centered and sample-SD
standardized; SD(b0)=SD(b1)=.9 and their correlation is +.5 or −.5. Residual SD
calibrates full-posterior slope reliability (.25 except .8 in the control).
Unequal information allocates half the people to 3 and half to 17 observations,
independently of latent effects/errors. The additional stratified comparator
preserves these counts; it is a study comparator, not a new package strata API.

**Arm A: noisy predictors.** Keep the previous structural outcome
Z=1.5+.4*b0+(gamma/.9)*b1+eta with Var(Z)=1 and Gaussian homoskedastic eta.
Fit both recovered intercept and slope as noisy predictors. Report the focal
slope coefficient/SE/endpoints multiplied by the population SD .9. The old
OLS-outcome stacked helper does not implement this estimator and is deliberately
absent from arm A.

**Arm B: random-slope outcome.** Extract the shared independent standard-normal
z from the original null structural outcome and construct
x_gamma=gamma*b1/.9+sqrt(1-gamma^2)*z. Joint normality gives
E[b1|x_gamma]=.9*gamma*x_gamma. Fit re(time)~x_gamma and divide the focal
coefficient/SE/endpoints by .9. The old stacked helper is evaluated unchanged,
using an ML measurement fit and OLS structural regression, HC0–HC3 and its
original t_(N−2) reference. REPAIR retains REML and uses normal Wald intervals
for its influence calculations. In balanced schedules common fixed-slope
centering cancels and M-MOM's weights are constant, yielding an exact OLS slope
anchor. Under unequal schedules M-MOM estimates precision weights whereas the
old helper uses unweighted OLS: the same population target, different estimators.
Its HC1 scaling uses the total stacked parameter count, as in the original code.
The legacy helper returns finite results even at some singular native fits; its
original behavior is preserved, rather than applying the new IF boundary gate.

The legacy helper is sourced from the research repository's
R/stacked_sandwich_helpers.R and R/derivative_backends.R. It is a simulation
comparator, not a new exported package inference method. The research code is
not copied into the MIT package. Its analytic backend computes an observed
score Hessian; a misleading expected-information label does not change the
executed comparator. Source hashes and fitting criteria are archived.

## What the new covariance estimates

For fixed total person frequency N, T(f,psi) denotes the canonical finite-sample
structural estimator. U_i=N*dT/df along the centered person-frequency direction.
The measurement influence is H^-1*S_i*, with H minus the average score Jacobian
and S_i* the centered frequency derivative of the native fitting score. D=dT/dpsi.
The full person influence is U_i+D*IF_psi,i. Its empirical outer product divided
by N^2 includes stage2, measurement and both signed cross-stage terms.

Measurement scores are analytic Gaussian scores; their Jacobian and the entire
structural sensitivity are numerically differentiated, with central/half-step,
one-sided and active-branch checks. For REML both the global fixed-design
information determinant and its person-frequency derivative are retained.
ML scores at a REML fit would propagate a different procedure. There are no
hidden HC corrections, pseudoinverses or ridges. All original point estimates
and ordinary conditional SEs remain unchanged.

Stage2 differentiates the full structural estimator with measurement quantities
fixed. It still re-estimates structural variance, weights and corrections and
therefore differs from the ordinary model-based conditional M-MOM SE. Stable
local regularization/floor branches are allowed and reported; neither numerical
stability nor a local derivative establishes uniform validity near a boundary.
Many noisy-predictor analyses occupy the forced-zero residual-variance branch.
The bootstrap can cross branches and captures a different finite-sample shape;
the poor local Wald coverage here cannot be resolved merely by adding a positive
measurement variance term or assuming that every full SE should increase.

## Availability

```{r availability, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'availability.png'))
```

```{r reasons}
x <- as.data.frame(with(s$diagnostics,table(measurement_singular,full)))
tab(x[x$Freq>0,])
```

All 1,048 singular-model refusals are intentional. The one other refusal is
arm B, low_larger, replication 68, gamma=.40: an unstable/branch-sensitive
measurement-parameter derivative at coordinate 6 (log residual SD). The original
stage2 result remains available. There were no driver, replay-reconstruction or
public-API errors. We retained the prespecified step/tolerance rather than tuning
them to maximize availability after viewing coverage.

Coverage and zero exclusion use **only available intervals**. The CSVs also
report interval-and-cover/detect per all 100 planned datasets. Missing intervals
are not valid non-rejections. Conditioning on availability selects a subset and
can change the apparent distribution; compare common eligible datasets too.

## Arm A: noisy predictors

```{r aplot, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'predictor_coverage.png'))
```

Nonzero effect: zero exclusion is detection, not a type-I error rate.

```{r aalt}
tab(compact('predictor',.4))
```

Null focal effect, conditional on the other noisy random coefficient:

```{r anull}
tab(compact('predictor',0))
```

Full influence versus full bootstrap, **coverage on common available datasets**:

```{r paired}
x <- subset(s$paired,arm=='predictor' & gamma==.4 & method_a=='Full influence Wald' &
            method_b=='Full person percentile' & metric=='covers')
tab(x[,c('profile','n','difference','mc_low','mc_high','a_only','b_only')])
```

Differences are IF minus bootstrap; bounds are normal paired Monte Carlo bounds,
based on per-dataset decision differences. Zero discordance yields no asserted
equivalence interval. All pairwise tables, including full vs conditional and
stage2, are retained. Per-method point bias, empirical SD, eligible bias/SD and
SE calibration appear in performance.csv. Conditional coverage can look high
because intervals are wide; the methods share the same original point estimates.

## Arm B: recovered random-slope outcome

```{r bplot, out.width='100%'}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(root,'outcome_coverage.png'))
```

```{r balt}
tab(compact('outcome',.4))
```

```{r bnull}
tab(compact('outcome',0))
```

HC3/t coverage was 95–97% across these nonzero-effect profiles and all 100 legacy
intervals/profile were finite. That is useful exploratory finite-sample evidence
for this **OLS-outcome** comparator; it is not validation for noisy-predictor
M-MOM and does not justify replacing REPAIR's SE with the old helper. The
unequal-design legacy width is larger partly because the point estimator is
unweighted OLS. Separately archived normal-critical legacy diagnostics isolate
the t reference from covariance changes. No claim of general HC3 superiority
follows from 100 reused replications/profile.

## Covariance decomposition and numerical sensitivity

Medians over available full results, pooling the two truths:

```{r decomposition}
tab(aggregate(cbind(full_to_stage2,measurement_fraction,cross_fraction)~profile+arm,
              s$components,median),digits=5)
```

In balanced arm B the focal measurement sensitivity cancels numerically; full
and stage2 are the same HC0 variance. In arm A the full/stage2 variance ratio
ranges roughly .79–3.62 across available analyses, so propagation can increase
or decrease uncertainty. The signed cross term is essential even when median
changes are modest. Per-dataset contributions, not just medians, are archived.

On the fixed first three datasets/profile (72 arm/effect checks), halving the
derivative step changed no availability decisions. Maximum matched relative
covariance changes were 1.35e-7 (full) and 1.19e-7 (stage2). This subset does not
establish stability of every refused full-grid derivative.

Across the 156 fixed-subset bootstrap comparisons (arms, truths and methods),
all B499 and B1999 intervals were available; one coverage decision changed from
uncovered to covered, none in the reverse direction. Full-person median sums of
absolute lower/upper endpoint changes were .0293 in arm A and .0421 in arm B.
The B499 arrays are exact prefixes of the B1999 arrays. This small tail check is
not a high-precision coverage study.

## Bootstrap reuse and validation

Arm A retains the exact previous robust native-refit bootstrap intervals and
draw maps. Arm B reuses those actual native optimizations, their convergence
decisions, person draws and refitted residual SDs. Every structural estimator is
recomputed per draw. Common measurement fixed-effect centering cancels from the
focal slope in this design, allowing cached focal computation; **intercept
bootstrap inference is not reconstructed or claimed**. Both full and frozen
measurement comparisons use the original complete-vector/failure gate, with no
deletion, replacement or silent acceptance of failed draws.

The first two datasets/profile, both arm-B outcomes, were checked against 24
complete public repair_bootstrap() calls at B99 (2,376 attempts). Draws,
complete-vector eligibility and focal estimates agreed, maximum focal error
6.66e-16. Identity repair_refit() checks also passed. Additional independent
validation recomputes coverage and zero exclusion from all 17,200 endpoints,
checks centering/ID alignment and covariance sums, OLS anchors, B prefixes and
frozen source/library/reference hashes.

```{r validation, results='asis'}
cat('```text\n',paste(readLines(file.path(root,'validation.txt')),collapse='\n'),'\n```\n',sep='')
```

## Reproduction and limits

The frozen numerical baseline is repair commit
558bdcead1c15cedd1e332aed6f01e86d49f3721, built on robust-refit head 7770874.
Later scope guards reject sample-wide formula/weight recipes; this study's
pointwise time models are unchanged. Final package checks separately validate
that guarded implementation against a fixed subset of recorded results.
The full study archive is local to blup_unshrinking under
vig_hallquist_2026/analysis/repair_bootstrap_pilot/influence_comparison; README.md
records commands, libraries, source dependencies and retained checkpoints.
The PR's dev/influence-simulation bundle permits endpoint-based verification
without a simulation rerun or private research code. It does not claim to
contain all native bootstrap histories.

This screen covers Gaussian iid errors, six fixed schedules/reliabilities and
two particular structural designs. It does not validate general heteroskedastic
measurement models, informative missingness, shared nuisance effects, nlme,
multiple measurement models, arbitrary adaptive transformations or nominal
coverage under all boundary sequences. The full sandwich is a coherent new
inference tool and diagnostic; these results argue against presenting it as a
universal replacement for bootstrap or ordinary conditional inference.
